subject: Summary: The alpha value for the regression

messages.author: 864fe5abb3987150
messages.subject: Summary: The alpha value for the regression
parts:
Thanks for the replies from Ken Burnham and Len Thomas for the questions:
“Why the default á (alpha) value for the regression regarding "cluster size
bias" is 0.15 instead of 0.05? How to set the appropriate alpha value?”



Summary:



First point: alpha=0.05 is traditional for tests, but is arbitrary in its
origins (once upon a time R.A. Fisher suggested it, but that was in the
spirit of 0.05 being the biggest P-value at which one would think maybe the
null hypothesis was to be considered false). Traditionally, also, this sort
of testing was for use in true experiments where there was a no-effects
null hypothesis and people wanted to demonstrate strong evidence against
the null (0.05 is not strong evidence, actually, in this context) if it was
to be considered "rejected.".



Second point: we do not have a true null about which we want or need strong
evidence. We really are here in more of a model selection context where a
trade-off of bias and variance is the issue. When testing has been used, as
in step-wise, for model selection it has been common to use P=0.15 as the
basis to "enter" a variable. This is partly a tradition in model selection,
but has some justification. If AIC were used here to choice between a model
with no effect of distance on detection probability vs. a one
slope-parameter regression model for a distance-effect than AIC, in this
case, acts like a test of that regression parameter (vs. 0) at alpha=0.15.
Thus, this alpha choice is also consistent with an AIC based selection.



Third - elaborate on aspect of #2. Initially we thought that using the
regression approach to dealing with cluster-size bias would entail
noticeable loss in precision for estimated expected cluster size if there
was no, or little, size-bias. But we found out that the regression-based
adjustment did not result in much increased variance over simple s-bar when
there was no size bias. However, there can be moderate to strong size bias
(in s-bar) with what seems like mild effects on detection probability as a
function of distance and cluster size. What this all means is that if in
doubt, adjust for possible size-bias effects because the expected gain can
be substantial while the expected loss is minor if there is no such
size-bias. Thus, in a testing context we should use a liberal alpha, such
as 0.15. So as a default, we did.



Fourth- elaborate on aspect of #2.

little is lost by applying the regression (only one extra parameter is
being estimated so precision is little worse than using the mean), and
there is often poor power to detect size bias, when doing analyses
stratified for cluster size.

Since you're doing a statistical test, the concept of statistical power is
germaine.

kind of trade-off between "type I error" and "type II error" that we do
not want to accept he wrong null hypothesis but we do not want to fail to
reject false null hypothesis, either.

One minor difference: the cost of a type II error in this context (ie
failing to detect size bias when it

exists) is a biased density estimate. The cost of a type I error
(incorrectly using the regression intercept when the mean would be a
better estimator of expected cluster size) is loss of precision. So, you
can couch it as a bias/precision trade-off, which is similar to the
argument Ken was making in the context of AIC.
